references.text: The continuation of the law concerning a thief who breaks in, clarifying when bloodguilt applies and when it does not.
Addresses blood vengeance and when killing is not considered murder, related to the concept of 'no bloodguilt'.
Explains that blood defiles the land and provides context for why innocent blood must be protected.
David is called a thief by Nabal, illustrating how theft was viewed in Israelite society.
Describes the thief who breaks in at night, paralleling the situation in Exodus 22:1.
Concerns a thief who steals and the consequences, including restitution for theft.
Refers to the blood of innocent poor people and thieves who break in.
Describes thieves coming at night and climbing in, similar to the burglary scenario.
Jesus uses the image of a thief breaking in at night as a parable about vigilance.
Paul uses the image of the thief coming at night to describe the day of the Lord.
A clear theological contrast between the general prohibition against murder and the specific exception for self-defense.
Repetition of the tenth commandment, creating a theological contrast with the exception rule for self-defense.
Direct theological contrast between the general penalty for murder and the exception in cases of self-defense.
